weaknesses: The central variance-reduction argument is not valid as presented. The appendix analyzes averaging numerical returns under i.i.d. rewards and gamma=1, whereas the algorithm averages gradients from different prefix-conditioned predictions. If the predictions were shared, squared-error gradient averaging would be equivalent to training against the averaged target and would not avoid reward dilution; if they are different predictions, the appendix does not apply. Correlated rewards, correlated bootstrap errors, and gradient covariance are ignored, and the derived variance still grows as O(N).

The mathematical specification is internally inconsistent. Equation 6 appears to use the same G^(n) target for every action prefix, while the following text says the outputs use G^(1),...,G^(n). The target value, entropy term, twin-critic minimum, terminal handling, padding, and precise policy-update input are not defined; the pseudocode and architecture show only one critic despite presenting the method as SAC.

Because the Transformer is causal, the first-token Q(s_t,a_t) used by the actor cannot attend to future action tokens. Longer-prefix predictions therefore act only as shared-parameter auxiliary tasks. The paper provides neither analysis nor direct evidence that this yields the claimed temporal reasoning, smooth global value surface, or continuous action sequences.

The core novelty is incremental relative to the cited TOP-ERL critic and prior temporally coordinated exploration work, yet neither TOP-ERL nor a matched n-step SAC baseline is evaluated. Other missing controls include a parameter-matched non-Transformer sequence critic, direct return averaging, varying horizon length, and removing future-action conditioning.

The empirical protocol is insufficient for strong claims: main-result seed counts, evaluation-episode counts, confidence intervals, and definitions of the plotted bands/IQM aggregation are absent. The claimed sparse box-pushing superiority is directly contradicted by Table 1, where gSDE scores 60% and T-SAC scores 58%.

Baseline fairness is unclear. Algorithms use markedly different update schedules, normalization, reward processing, network sizes, discount factors, and entropy settings; on box-pushing T-SAC sets the entropy coefficient to zero and is therefore not actually the stated soft actor-critic method. No equal-compute comparison, tuning budget, runtime, parameter count, or sensitivity analysis is reported.

The ablations use selectively chosen and differing task subsets, provide few numerical summaries, and do not cleanly separate the Transformer, multi-step targets, critic-side action prefixes, and policy modifications. Consequently, the large headline gains cannot be attributed to the proposed critic mechanism.

The paper conflates Meta-World ML1, all-50-task aggregation, and generalization, without specifying the held-out goal/task protocol. Together with the absence of code and several essential implementation details, this substantially limits reproducibility and leaves the state-of-the-art and sample-efficiency claims unsupported.

There is a fundamental disconnect between the proposed action-chunk critic and the policy update. Equation 8 optimizes only Q(s_t,a_t). Under the stated causal mask, this first-token output cannot depend on future action tokens, so it is unclear how the actor directly benefits from evaluating action chunks. At most, later-token losses provide shared-parameter auxiliary supervision, which is materially weaker than the paper's central temporal-reasoning narrative.

The mathematical and algorithmic specification is internally inconsistent. Equation 6 appears to compare every prefix output against G^(n), despite the surrounding text claiming targets G^(1),...,G^(n). The paper also does not adequately define the target soft value, twin-critic/minimum operation, terminal handling, sequence padding, horizon sampling, or how the critic is invoked during actor updates. The experiments conflate the proposed critic with many other changes: trajectory replay, multi-step supervision, policy layer normalization, mean-conditioned covariance, optimizer and network changes, buffer size, warm-up, and update schedule. In box-pushing, T-SAC additionally uses zero entropy regularization while SAC uses automatic entropy tuning, and discount factors and update counts differ. Missing central ablations include one-step versus multi-step Transformer critics, MLP multi-horizon critics, target- versus gradient-level averaging, context-length sensitivity, and parameter/compute-matched models.

The statistical evidence is insufficient for the strong claims. The sparse box-pushing claim is directly contradicted by Table 1: T-SAC scores 58%, below gSDE at 60%. No box-pushing learning curves or uncertainty estimates are provided, so the claimed sparse-reward state of the art is unsupported.

weaknesses: The central credit-assignment interpretation is not technically convincing. The actor uses only Q(s,a), whose causally masked first output receives a one-step target; longer returns supervise different functions conditioned on future action prefixes. They therefore constitute shared-parameter auxiliary tasks, not N-step backups of the action value used by the actor. No theory establishes beneficial transfer to that first output, and no equal-compute control separates this transfer from simply using more targets and optimization.

The claimed target-free method is not target-free: it snapshots the online critic, freezes that copy for K updates, and uses it for bootstrap targets. This is a conventional target network with periodic hard updates, also explicitly represented as phi_target in Algorithm 1. Consequently, the conceptual claim of eliminating target networks is misleading.

The theoretical analysis is poorly aligned with the implemented method. Appendix C studies averaging targets even though the paper states that T-SAC does not do this. Appendix D assumes unverified homoscedastic, positively equicorrelated horizon gradients and treats gradients of different objectives as if averaging them were an unbiased variance-reduction operation. Appendix G analyzes multiple starting states sharing one terminal bootstrap, whereas Equations 5–7 use one starting state and a different bootstrap state for each horizon. These results do not substantiate the main algorithmic claims.

The headline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Most Meta-World baselines are imported from prior publications or official runs under settings described only as 'comparable,' rather than rerun under the same evaluation pipeline. Protocol alignment for the unusual final-timestep success criterion is not demonstrated, seed counts differ substantially, CrossQ is capped at 10M steps on Box-Pushing while T-SAC receives 20M, and T-SAC receives extensive benchmark-specific tuning without a held-out selection protocol.

Several method descriptions and claims are inconsistent. The critic omits the entropy term required by the stated maximum-entropy SAC Bellman objective, and the key Box-Pushing configuration sets the entropy coefficient to zero. The paper also describes independent ML1 task training as testing task generalization, although ML1 does not evaluate cross-task generalization.

The evidence is presented mainly as learning curves, without exact endpoint or AUC tables, paired comparisons, or a clear description of the bootstrap unit. Important sparse-reward and ablation conclusions use only four seeds, while the proposed per-task-then-average IQM aggregation is nonstandard and insufficiently justified.

Reproducibility remains limited because code and trained models are only promised after acceptance. This is particularly consequential given the inconsistencies among the equations, algorithm, and Appendix G, the extensive tuning, and the lack of exact provenance for imported baseline curves. Overall, the results are promising but do not adequately support the paper's novelty, target-free, theoretical, or state-of-the-art claims.

strengths: The prefix-conditioned causal Transformer critic is an interesting way to use realized action sequences for multi-horizon supervision without importance weighting while retaining a one-step policy.
The empirical study is broad: 57 tasks across Meta-World, Box-Pushing, and MuJoCo, with particularly strong sample efficiency on Meta-World and strong dense Box-Pushing performance.

The paper reports per-task curves, bootstrap confidence intervals, runtime measurements, several architectural and horizon ablations, and candidly identifies weaker locomotion and sparse-reward results.
The appendices provide extensive environment, reward, and hyperparameter descriptions.
weaknesses: The main mechanism is not convincingly established. Under the causal mask, the Q(s,a) used by the actor cannot access later actions; multi-step outputs therefore affect policy learning only indirectly through shared parameters. Ablations do not adequately separate this auxiliary-training effect from architecture, parameter count, tuning, or increased supervision.

The theoretical contribution has substantial problems. Averaging gradients is simply optimizing the mean loss; gradients for different horizons generally have different expectations, undermining the claimed unbiased variance comparison. The later theorem invokes target averaging that the paper explicitly says T-SAC does not use. Appendix C also incorrectly claims convergence of the reward-side variance ratio to 4 for gamma=1 including rho=0, where the limit is 3, and makes unsupported claims about cross-covariances.

The claimed target-network-free method is not target-free: snapshotting a critic, freezing it for K updates, and using cached bootstrap values is functionally a hard-updated target network, essentially the standard DQN mechanism. Thus a prominent headline contribution is misleading.

The algorithm is insufficiently specified and internally inconsistent: it does not state whether T-SAC uses twin critics or clipped minimization, does not specify how the bootstrap expectation is estimated, mixes a non-soft critic with a SAC actor without analyzing the resulting objective, and contains multiple off-by-one inconsistencies in its sequence and window definitions.

The evidence for attribution is weak. Most ablations use only four seeds on dense Box-Pushing, sometimes with different interaction budgets, and there is no corresponding component ablation on the headline Meta-World aggregate. Figure 5e appears to show one sampled window learning fastest, contrary to the text's claim that multiple windows help. The causal-mask and horizon sweeps also show limited or overlapping improvements.

The state-of-the-art comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Many Meta-World baselines are imported from prior publications, use 4–20 seeds, different budgets, normalization choices, architectures, and tuning effort, whereas T-SAC receives a targeted grid search. Evaluation episode counts for Meta-World and Box-Pushing are not reported, and the unusual per-task-IQM-then-average aggregation further complicates comparison.

The contribution is incremental relative to TOP-ERL and action-sequence critics, while the paper overstates consistency: T-SAC is weak on several MuJoCo tasks and remains below TOP-ERL on sparse Box-Pushing.

Reproducibility remains limited because code is deferred until acceptance, and the promised search grids and exact seed lists are not actually supplied; several update-count, UTD, and epoch definitions are also unclear.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving credit assignment in long-horizon continuous-control tasks while retaining a step-based policy.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering 50 Meta-World tasks, five MuJoCo tasks, and dense/sparse Box-Pushing. Learning curves, IQM aggregation, confidence intervals, runtime measurements, and several negative results are reported.
The dense Box-Pushing and Meta-World results are promising, including strong performance on difficult multi-stage tasks.
The ablations examine horizon length, attention components, recurrent alternatives, action chunking, and sampling frequency. Hyperparameter and environment appendices are extensive.
Conditioning the auxiliary value predictions on realized replay action prefixes is a reasonable way to avoid importance sampling for that particular sequence-value estimand.
weaknesses: The central characterization as N-step SAC is misleading. With causal attention, the Q(s,a) output used by the actor receives only a one-step TD target; longer-horizon outputs condition on future replay actions and represent different sequence-value functions. They influence Q(s,a) only indirectly through shared parameters. Thus the method is better understood as auxiliary multi-horizon representation learning, and the claimed long-horizon policy-credit mechanism lacks a derivation or direct validation.

Appendix G analyzes a different update from Equations 5–7: it assumes multiple suffix targets sharing one bootstrap state, whereas the main method uses a common start state and a different bootstrap for every prefix horizon. Its length-one case also produces zero updates, revealing an indexing inconsistency. Consequently, the target-reuse and quadratic sparse-reward propagation explanations do not apply to the stated algorithm.

The target-free claim is incorrect. The method explicitly copies the online critic into a frozen target snapshot and refreshes it every K updates; Algorithm 1 maintains a target critic. This is a conventional hard-updated target network, closely related to the long-established DQN mechanism, rather than a CrossQ-style target-free method.

The variance analysis is not convincing support for the algorithm. Averaging the gradients of the mean multi-horizon loss is algebraically automatic; the analysis assumes homoscedastic, equicorrelated gradients without evidence, even though the horizons optimize different quantities and need not share a common expectation. It also invokes target averaging that the implementation explicitly does not use.

The experimental comparison is not sufficiently controlled. Many Meta-World baselines are imported from prior work with varying seeds, budgets, implementations, and only asserted-to-be-comparable protocols, while T-SAC receives a targeted grid search and several additional design changes. Exact alignment of environment versions, train/test goal splits, evaluation episodes, and final-timestep success definitions is not established.

Interaction budgets are matched more clearly than computation or supervision budgets: every Transformer update can contain many horizon losses, and the method samples multiple windows per environment step. The nominal UTD therefore obscures substantially different amounts of critic supervision. The ablation evidence is concentrated on one dense Box-Pushing task and does not establish which components drive the broader gains.

As written, the algorithm also departs materially from SAC by using an unregularized bootstrap value and apparently a single critic, without the soft Bellman target or clipped twin critics. No derivation shows that the resulting actor/critic objectives optimize the stated maximum-entropy objective, and these changes are not separately ablated.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: code is promised only after acceptance, and important implementation details such as expectation estimation in V(s), exact update-count accounting, terminal-segment handling, and the relationship between the reported UTD values and tabled update counts are unclear. Overall, the empirical signal is interesting, but the method description, theory, novelty claims, and evaluation controls require substantial correction before the work is competitive at a top-tier venue.

Twin-critic handling, target-action estimation, and several terminal/masking details are underspecified.

The central off-policy argument is incomplete. Avoiding importance sampling is achieved by redefining later outputs around recorded action prefixes; in stochastic environments, future behavior actions are correlated with intervening states that the critic does not observe, so these targets need not estimate interventional action-sequence values. Moreover, the actor uses only Q(s,a), whose causal first-token output receives a one-step target; longer-horizon targets affect it only indirectly through shared parameters. Thus the claimed N-step credit-assignment mechanism is not established.

The theoretical analysis does not convincingly support the implemented method. Averaging gradients of different horizon-specific losses is simply optimizing their mean, and those gradients estimate different objectives, so standard variance-reduction and unbiased-estimator arguments do not directly apply. The target-averaging analysis concerns a procedure the method explicitly does not use. There are also concrete errors or overclaims: for example, with gamma=1 and zero reward correlation, the stated variance ratio approaches 3 rather than 4.

The claimed target-free contribution is misleading: snapshotting a critic, caching its targets, and refreshing it every K steps is functionally a periodically hard-updated target-network scheme, not elimination of target networks.

The evaluation is not sufficiently controlled for the strongest claims. Most Meta-World baselines are imported from prior runs with differing seeds, budgets, normalization, and hyperparameters, while T-SAC receives a substantial task-specific search. Code is promised only after acceptance, exact search grids and seed identities are absent, and the sparse result uses only four seeds. Figure 5e also appears to contradict the accompanying claim: one sampled window learns fastest, whereas the default four-window setting is slowest.

MuJoCo results are mixed—CrossQ is clearly stronger on several tasks—and TOP-ERL remains better on sparse Box-Pushing, so claims of consistent superiority and broad state-of-the-art performance are overstated.

Because the critic omits entropy from its targets and the manuscript never clearly specifies clipped double-Q estimation, the method differs materially from SAC. This design may be viable, but it needs a precise objective, justification, and ablation rather than relying mainly on analogies to other algorithms.

strengths: The core design—a causal Transformer critic trained on realized action prefixes with multi-horizon supervision while retaining one-step policy updates—is intuitive and potentially useful for long-horizon control.
The evaluation is broad, covering 50 Meta-World tasks, five MuJoCo tasks, and dense and sparse Box-Pushing, with multiple seeds, bootstrap intervals, and per-task curves.
Results are particularly promising on multi-phase Meta-World tasks and dense Box-Pushing, where the reported 96.8% success rate is strong.
The paper includes useful ablations of horizon length, causal masking, attention, recurrent alternatives, target sampling, and policy-side chunking, as well as runtime and hyperparameter information.
The presentation is generally clear, and the authors disclose weaker locomotion and sparse-reward results rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: The central claim that conditioning on realized action prefixes eliminates the need for importance sampling is not established for general stochastic MDPs. Later behavior actions depend on intermediate states, so conditioning replay trajectories on those actions changes the transition distribution; without further assumptions, the learned multi-step quantity can remain behavior-policy dependent. The experiments largely use deterministic simulators, but the paper states the claim generally.

The claimed “target-free” method is not target-free: it snapshots the online critic, freezes that copy, caches bootstrap values, and refreshes it periodically. This is a conventional hard-updated target network, making the comparison and claimed contribution relative to CrossQ misleading.

The theoretical appendices have substantive problems. Averaged gradients correspond to different horizon-specific objectives, so treating them as interchangeable unbiased estimators is unjustified; the analysis also invokes unverified homoscedastic/equicorrelation assumptions and discusses target averaging that T-SAC explicitly does not use. Proposition 1 incorrectly claims a limit of 4 for all nonnegative correlations when the independent case approaches 3, and Appendix G's window definition yields zero updates for length one, contradicting the algorithm and exposing an off-by-one error.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the proposed mechanism from numerous simultaneous changes, including a non-soft critic, actor LayerNorm, unusual initial policy variances and target entropies, policy delays, warmups, optimizer changes, and different network capacities. A parameter- and compute-matched MLP with the same prefix losses is especially important because the actor only uses the first causally masked output, which cannot access later sequence tokens.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled: much of Meta-World uses curves imported from prior work with heterogeneous implementations and seed counts, Box-Pushing budgets differ, and several ablations use shorter budgets. Direct comparisons to corrected multi-step SAC, a rigorous action-chunking baseline, and stronger contemporary off-policy methods are missing.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. T-SAC is middling or worse than baselines on multiple MuJoCo tasks and trails TOP-ERL on sparse Box-Pushing, despite the abstract claiming consistent superiority. Meta-World ML1 trains separate agents per task and therefore does not substantiate the stated task-generalization claim.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: code is promised only after acceptance, seeds are not enumerated, and evaluation frequency and episode counts for Meta-World and Box-Pushing are insufficiently specified. Given the theoretical issues and non-unified comparisons, the impressive empirical results are not yet reliable enough for acceptance.

strengths: The prefix-conditioned critic is an intuitively useful construction: causal masking prevents future-action leakage, and conditioning on recorded action prefixes provides a plausible way to use multi-step supervision without importance sampling.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering 50 Meta-World tasks, five MuJoCo tasks, and dense and sparse Box-Pushing, generally with multiple seeds, confidence intervals, per-task curves, runtime measurements, and several ablations.

The paper provides extensive environment, reward, architecture, and hyperparameter details and candidly reports weaknesses such as sparse-reward instability and poor performance on some locomotion tasks.
The results suggest that multi-horizon auxiliary supervision can improve difficult manipulation tasks, even if the paper does not yet isolate why.
weaknesses: The main theoretical justification does not establish the claimed mechanism. Appendix C analyzes averaging N-step targets, which the method explicitly does not use. Appendix D then conflates averaging gradients of different horizon-specific objectives with variance reduction for an unbiased estimator of one objective, relying on unverified exchangeability and common-gradient assumptions; its claimed compounded target-smoothing benefit is not implemented.

The algorithm is internally inconsistent. Equations 5–7 bootstrap each prefix at a different state s_{t+i}, whereas Appendix G analyzes all updates in a window bootstrapping at one fixed endpoint s_q. Consequently, the stated target-reuse and quadratic sparse-reward-propagation explanations do not apply to the main objective. The freezing schedule also differs between Section 4.4, Algorithm 1, and the hyperparameter presentation.

During policy optimization, the critic is queried only as Q(s,a). Under the causal mask, this first-position output cannot attend to subsequent actions, so sequence modeling affects the policy only indirectly through shared-parameter auxiliary training. The paper nevertheless attributes improvements directly to sequence-aware long-horizon valuation without a compute- and capacity-matched MLP trained with the same prefix losses.

The method is not theoretically consistent with the stated SAC objective: the critic omits future entropy while the actor uses entropy regularization, but no policy-improvement or convergence argument is given. Moreover, Box-Pushing sets T-SAC's entropy coefficient to zero while the SAC baseline uses automatic entropy tuning, making both the name and comparison questionable.

Baseline fairness is inadequate. Most Meta-World baselines come from prior runs and were not comparably retuned, whereas T-SAC received a substantial grid search. On Box-Pushing, T-SAC also uses a much larger policy than SAC, different entropy settings, and up to 20M interactions, while CrossQ is stopped at 10M. These confounds prevent attributing gains to the proposed critic.

The conclusions overstate the evidence. CrossQ is better on most MuJoCo tasks, T-SAC is explicitly weak on Hopper and Walker2d, TOP-ERL reaches about 70% sparse Box-Pushing success versus T-SAC's 58%, and the target-free hard-copy variant undergoes severe late-training collapse. Thus the claimed consistent superiority and broad target-free stability are not supported.

Key ablations use only four seeds and only dense Box-Pushing; varying horizon length also changes the number of supervised outputs and computation. Final numerical tables, probability-of-improvement analyses, and uncertainty for headline differences are absent.

Reproducibility remains limited because code is promised only after acceptance, while important details—target caching and refresh semantics, exact UTD accounting, bootstrap-value computation, and which of the contradictory target definitions is implemented—are unclear. Overall, the idea is plausible and the empirical signal is interesting, but the soundness, attribution, novelty, and evaluation gaps are too substantial for acceptance.

Averaging gradients of different horizon losses has the usual variance-of-a-mean property under strong equicorrelation assumptions, but those gradients optimize different objectives, so unbiasedness, convergence, and uniform-weight optimality do not follow.

Algorithm 1 stops segment collection at termination, while Figure 12 concatenates episodes. Appendix G's indexing makes a length-one window contain zero TD updates, conflicting with its comparison to one-step TD. It is therefore unclear which procedure produced the results.

The actor and bootstrap value use only the first output Q(s,a). Under the causal mask, that output cannot access later action tokens; longer-horizon supervision influences it only indirectly through shared parameters. The method departs materially from SAC without adequate justification: it removes entropy from critic targets, describes only a single critic rather than clipped double Q-learning, leaves the computation of the action expectation in V unspecified, and reports an entropy coefficient of zero for Box-Pushing. These choices confound attribution and undermine the SAC framing.

The main Meta-World comparison is not controlled. Most baselines are imported from prior publications or released runs described merely as 'comparable,' with different seed counts, tuning, normalization, and potentially evaluation protocols. T-SAC receives an extensive task-specific search, while several baselines are not rerun or similarly tuned; Box-Pushing also uses a much larger four-layer 512-unit T-SAC actor than the principal step-based baselines.

The empirical claims are substantially stronger than the plots support. T-SAC is weaker than standard baselines on Hopper and Walker2d and not best on Ant, while sparse Box-Pushing reaches 58% versus the reported 70% for TOP-ERL and shows severe instability. Thus 'consistently outperforms' and broad state-of-the-art claims are unsupported.

Critical attribution baselines are missing: a capacity- and compute-matched MLP trained on exactly the same prefix targets, a Transformer trained only with one-step targets, standard multi-step alternatives such as TD(lambda)/Retrace-style corrections, and controlled comparisons of hard versus soft target updates. Existing ablations mix architecture, objectives, action chunking, and training budgets.

Reproducibility is insufficient for resolving these issues. Code is deferred until acceptance, promised search grids/configurations are absent, several essential implementation choices are unspecified, and UTD accounting is inconsistent: the Meta-World table gives 100 critic updates per 500 newly collected transitions, which is 0.2 under the same accounting that yields the stated 0.25 and 0.75 for Box-Pushing and MuJoCo, not the claimed UTD of 1.

Novelty is limited by the close combination of existing Transformer critics, action-prefix/chunk value functions, multi-step auxiliary supervision, and SAC; the additional hard-copy schedule is standard target-network practice. Given the unsupported central claims, mismatched theory, ambiguous algorithm, and uncontrolled evaluation, the issues are fundamental rather than readily repairable presentation gaps.

The paper lacks the decisive matched baseline: an MLP or other non-attention critic trained with the same causal prefix-conditioned multi-horizon objective, parameter budget, and sampling scheme. The reported fixed one-step and no-causal-mask ablations also approach similar final success, weakening the claimed mechanism.

The novelty over TOP-ERL is incremental: the paper adopts essentially the same lightweight Transformer-critic idea and truncated multi-step supervision, chiefly adapting it to a step-based actor. Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Most Meta-World results are imported from prior publications or released runs, with different seed counts, interaction budgets, implementations, and tuning effort, whereas T-SAC receives an extensive grid search. On Box-Pushing, CrossQ is capped at 10M interactions while T-SAC runs for 20M. Identical evaluation code and compute- or tuning-matched comparisons are not demonstrated.

Several changes from SAC are confounded with the proposed critic: a non-soft critic, policy LayerNorm, policy delay, temperature warmup, specialized replay sampling, and task-specific exploration settings. In particular, combining ordinary reward-return evaluation with an entropy-regularized SAC actor is not derived as optimizing the stated maximum-entropy objective and is not ablated.

The paper overstates empirical consistency. CrossQ is stronger on most MuJoCo tasks, and T-SAC is substantially worse than standard SAC/CrossQ on Hopper and Walker2d; TOP-ERL also exceeds T-SAC on sparse Box-Pushing (70% versus 58%). Accordingly, claims of consistently outperforming strong off-policy baselines or broadly achieving state of the art are not supported.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the extensive tables. Code is promised only after acceptance, while essential details are ambiguous: whether twin critics and clipped minima are used, how the bootstrap expectation is approximated, and how terminal targets are handled. The K=20 frozen-target schedule in Section 4.4 is not reconciled with Algorithm 1 or the hyperparameter tables, and the stated UTD ratios are difficult to recover from the listed collection and update counts.

Central sparse-reward and ablation results use only four seeds and often have wide confidence intervals, without numerical result tables or formal paired comparisons. All evaluations are fully observed simulated control tasks, so claims about trajectory context, generalization, and broad long-horizon applicability remain insufficiently tested.
